chapters.title: Chapter 1 · The Building of the Wall
chapters.artPrompt: a giant in rough furs and a great shaggy horse hauling huge stone blocks up a high wall around a shining city on a mountaintop, gods watching from golden palaces, low northern sun, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Long ago, the Gods built their home on the top of a high mountain. They called their shining City Asgard, which means the Place of the Gods. The Giants were their old enemies, who wished to destroy the world and the race of men. So the Gods wanted the strongest wall ever built around Asgard. One day, a strange being came walking up the mountain. Odin, the Father of the Gods, went to speak with him. The stranger said that he could build a wall no enemy could ever break. It would take him one year, and not a day more.

New word: Asgard — the shining City of the Gods, built on the top of a high mountain. A rainbow bridge called Bifrost joins it to the world of men. The Giants, who live in a cold land beyond, are its old enemies.

Odin was glad, for a strong wall would let the Gods go out and help men. The stranger swore a great oath to finish the wall by the first day of summer. He brought no helper with him but one great horse. That horse worked wonders, hauling stones day and night and setting them in their places. Then Odin asked what payment he would claim. The answer was terrible. He asked for the Sun and the Moon, and for Freya, the gentle goddess who watches over flowers and grasses. Now the Gods knew that the stranger was one of the Giants.
The strange Giant and his great horse pile stones for the wall around Asgard.

The Gods would rather have no wall at all than lose the Sun, the Moon, and Freya. But Loki, the sly one who lived among the Gods, had a plan. Let the Giant build on, he said, and let the Gods swear one thing more. If the last stone was not laid by the first day of summer, no payment at all would be given. The wall rose higher and higher, and three days before summer only one stone over the gateway was missing. Then Loki changed himself into a pretty little mare. She galloped past the Giant's great horse in the moonlight. The tired horse dropped his stone and ran after her over the meadows. He never came back to the wall again.

Who is Loki? He is the sly and clever one who lives among the Gods, though his father was a Giant of the wind. He can change his shape into a bird, a fish, or a horse. His tricks sometimes help the Gods, and sometimes bring them great trouble.

The first day of summer came, and the gateway still stood unfinished. The Giant had hunted all night for his horse, and he had not found him. "Your work is not finished," Odin said. "You forced us to a hard bargain, and now we need not keep it." Then the Giant flew into a rage and tried to tear down the palaces. But the Gods laid hands on him and thrust him outside his own great wall. "Go, and trouble Asgard no more," Odin commanded. Loki came home and told how he had led the great horse away. The Gods rejoiced behind their strong new wall. But Odin sat sad upon his throne, for a trick had been played and an oath had been broken.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 · Iduna and Her Apples
chapters.artPrompt: a huge dark eagle carrying a gentle goddess holding a basket of golden apples across icy mountains and a starry sky, a rainbow bridge far below, storybook illustration

blocks.text: In a garden of Asgard there grew a tree with shining apples. Whoever ate one of those apples never grew a day older. The Goddess Iduna tended the tree, and only she might pick the apples. Every morning she filled her basket, and every day the Gods and Goddesses came to eat and stay young. Iduna never left her garden, for the tree would grow no apples without her care. One day Odin went traveling through the world of men, and he took Loki with him. The two grew hungry in a cold empty land, and Loki caught a young bull to roast.

New word: Iduna — the gentle Goddess who keeps a basket of golden apples. Whoever eats one of her apples each day never grows older. Without her and her apples, even the Gods would grow gray and weak.

But by some Giant's magic the meat would not cook. A mighty eagle came circling over the fire and offered to cook it for a share. The eagle flapped his wings until the fire blazed, and at last the meat was done. Then he seized piece after piece, till hardly any was left for Loki. Loki struck at him with the spit in his anger. The spit stuck fast to the eagle, and Loki could not let go. The great bird rose into the sky with Loki hanging on. He flew with him over the ice and rocks of Joetunheim, the Realm of the Giants, and left him there.

The eagle was the Giant Thiassi in that shape, and he had caught Loki at last. He said that Loki might go home only if he brought him Iduna's shining apples. Cold and miserable, Loki swore to do it. Back in Asgard, he told Iduna that he had seen apples elsewhere, brighter and sweeter than hers. Simple, trusting Iduna wept to hear it. "Go and see for yourself," said cunning Loki. "The tree stands just outside the wall." So Iduna carried her basket beyond the gate of Asgard. A mighty eagle swooped down and carried her away over the world, toward the Giants' land.
The great eagle carries Iduna and her basket of shining apples far away from Asgard.
Joetunheim is the Realm of the Giants, a land of ice, rock, and dark mountains. No green things grow there, and fire bursts out of the ground. Its name means the home of the mighty Giant folk.

Without her apples, a change came over the Dwellers in Asgard. They walked slowly, their shoulders bent, and their eyes lost their brightness. Age was coming upon the Gods. Then Odin's two ravens flew home and told him where Iduna was hidden. Thor seized Loki, and Loki begged for one more chance. He borrowed a dress of falcon feathers and flew to the Giants' land. He changed Iduna into a sparrow, and they flew toward Asgard together, the great eagle behind them. The Gods lit great fires on the wall. Loki darted through the flames, but Thiassi could find no way through, and he fell down from the wall. Then Iduna gave out her apples again, and youth came back to Asgard.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 · Sif's Golden Hair
chapters.artPrompt: a little misshapen dwarf working bellows in a glowing cave while a gadfly stings his hand, sparks and molten gold flying, a shining hammer on the anvil, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The Gods were still angry with Loki for the loss of Iduna. One day he found Sif, the wife of Thor, asleep outside her house. Her beautiful golden hair flowed all around her, and Thor loved it dearly. Smiling, Loki took out his shears and cut off every strand. Sif did not wake until her treasure was gone. When Thor came home, his wife hid her bare head in shame. She said she would go away and live among the Dwarfs, for she could not bear to be seen. Then Thor's anger rose like a storm.

Thor dragged Loki before the Council of the Gods, and Odin spoke sternly. Loki must restore the beauty of Sif's hair. So Loki went down, down through winding passages under the earth, to the caves where the Dwarfs work their forges. The Dwarfs are the best craftsmen in the world, though they are little, twisted, and ugly. Loki praised their work until they would refuse him nothing. They took a bar of fine gold and hammered it into threads as fine as hairs. The golden web they made fell soft over Sif's shorn head and held there like growing hair. All Asgard clapped its hands for joy.

New word: Dwarfs — little twisted craftsmen who live in caves under the earth. They are ugly to look at, but no one in the world can beat them at smith's work. Their forges burn day and night beneath the ground.

Loki also carried off a spear that never misses its mark, and a magic boat that folds small as cloth. He gave the spear to Odin and the boat to Frey. Then he boasted that no other Dwarfs could make such wonders. But a Dwarf named Brock stood in the shadow, trembling with rage. His brother Sindri, he cried, was the best smith of all. Brock wagered his own head that his brother's work was better, and Loki took the bet. The Gods sat down to judge between them.
In the smoky forge, little Brock works the bellows while the gadfly stings his hand.

In Sindri's glowing forge, Brock worked the bellows and kept the fire just so. A gadfly flew in and stung his hands, and stung again, but Brock never stopped. First came a golden boar that shines as it flies through the air. Next came an armring from which eight new rings of gold drop every ninth night. Last, Sindri threw in a bar of iron. The gadfly stung Brock between the eyes, and blood blinded him for one moment. The fire sank, and the hammer's handle came out a little too short. Still it was Mjollnir, the greatest thing the Dwarfs ever made.

Mjollnir is the name of Thor's great hammer. It is short in the handle, yet it always strikes the mark and always comes back to Thor's hand. It is the strongest weapon the Gods own, the defence of Asgard.

The Gods looked at the golden boar and the bright armring, and they wondered. But when Thor swung the hammer Mjollnir round his head, a great cry went up. With that hammer in his hand, no one could stand against the Champion of Asgard. So judgment was given for Brock, and Loki's head was forfeit. Loki knelt and smiled. "Take my head, but do not touch my neck," he said. "You never bargained for that." The Dwarf could not take the head without the neck. So in triumph he sewed Loki's lips together with a thong. For a long time after, there was peace in Asgard from mischief.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 · Freya's Necklace
chapters.artPrompt: a fair goddess in flowing robes standing before three grim Giant Women on a misty mountaintop as they hold up a glowing golden necklace, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Freya, the fairest of the Goddesses, had seen the golden wonders Loki brought to Asgard. Now she dreamed day and night of shining things she might own. In the old days three Giant Women had come to Asgard, and gold had flashed through their hands. They were banished long ago, but Freya could not forget them. She did not tell Odur, her husband, for he loved the old happy days when no one hoarded gold. "I shall not love him the less because I go my own way for once," she said to herself.

New word: Freya — the gentle Goddess who watches over the flowers and the grasses. She rides in a car drawn by two cats. The Vanir, her people, are a bright and friendly race who are friends of the Gods.

One day she left her palace and her little child Hnossa, and went down to the earth. She asked the way to the mountaintop where the three Giant Women sat. The Elves would not tell her. The Dwarfs below the earth knew the way. They would show it only if she stayed with them till morning. So Freya stayed, and she was sad and ashamed. At last she stood before the three, in the shadow of their high seats. One of them held up a necklace more beautiful than anything ever made by hands. "It is the necklace Brisingamen," she said. "It is yours to wear, wife of Odur."
Freya stands in the shadow of the Giant Women as they hold up the shining necklace Brisingamen.

Freya clasped the necklace round her throat and went home shining. But the house was quiet, and little Hnossa turned away crying. Odur was gone, and no one knew where. Then the Goddess Frigga came to her. "Odur left Asgard," said Frigga, "when you chose a shining thing above him." So Freya set out in her car drawn by two cats. Year after year she searched the whole world for him. She found no trace of her husband anywhere.

At last she turned her car toward the Rainbow Bridge, and there stood Heimdall, the Watcher for the Gods. "Tell me where Odur is," she cried. "Odur is in every place the searcher has not come," said Heimdall, "and in every place the searcher has left." Then Freya stood on the bridge and wept. When she looked up, her little daughter Hnossa stood there grown, more beautiful than any maiden in the world. Freya was comforted, and she went home with her child. Still she wears the necklace, but now as a sign of her sorrow. Her tears fall on the earth, and every tear becomes a drop of gold.

Brisingamen is the name of Freya's famous necklace. It was the most beautiful thing ever made by hands, and it made her more lovely still. But in this story it also brought her the greatest sorrow of her life.

chapters.title: Chapter 5 · Frey and Gerda
chapters.artPrompt: a tall noble god on horseback before a lonely house in a snowy land, a beautiful maiden standing in the warm lit doorway, northern stars above, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Frey, the chief of the Vanir, missed his sister Freya, who was wandering far away. He climbed the steps of Hlidskjalf, Odin's lofty watchtower, though no God but Odin might sit there. From the top he could look out over the whole world. He saw Midgard, the world of men, and beyond it Joetunheim with its dark mountains and its snow. Then the door of a lonely house opened, and a Giant maiden stood in the doorway. Her face was so beautiful that it was like starlight in that dark land. Frey gazed and gazed, and he went home with a heavy heart.

New word: Hlidskjalf — Odin's high watchtower in Asgard. From his seat at the top, the All-Father can look out over the whole world. No other God may sit in that seat, and Frey's sitting there brings him sorrow.

That night he could not sleep, and in the morning the wolves before the tower barred his way. His father, wise Nioerd, shook his head when he heard the tale. The maiden was Gerda, daughter of the Giant Gymer. To win her, Frey would have to give up what he prized most. What he prized most was his magic sword. His father warned him of the day of Ragnaroek, when the Giants will make war upon the Gods. "The day is far off," said Frey, "and I cannot live without Gerda."

So Frey gave his sword to Skirnir, his bold and reckless servant, and sent him to woo the Giant maid. Skirnir rode a mighty horse over the Rainbow Bridge, through monstrous wolves, and through a wall of burning fire. He showed Gerda gold and jewels, but she would not have them. He raised the magic sword, and she only laughed at him. Then he sang a terrible spell over her, of withering and sorrow, till she threw herself on the ground. "Spare me," she cried, "and I will give my love to Frey." Nine nights from that day, she promised, she would meet him in Barri Wood.
Skirnir on his mighty horse speaks to beautiful Gerda at the door of her father's house.

Ragnaroek is the Twilight of the Gods, the last battle that the old stories tell of. On that day the Giants will march against Asgard. The wise Gods try to be ready for it, but no one knows when it will come.

Nine nights are long to a lover. "Long is one day, and long, long two," said Frey. But the ninth evening came at last, and in Barri Wood he met Gerda the beautiful. They gave each other rings of gold, and it was settled that she should come as a bride to Asgard. All the Gods came to love gentle Gerda. Yet the price of her love was never forgotten. Frey had no sword, and old Nioerd remembered the prophecy. When the last battle comes, they say, Frey will stand in that fight without a weapon in his hand.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 · Heimdall and All Things
chapters.artPrompt: a golden-toothed watchman beside a glowing rainbow bridge telling stories to a small child, the great World Tree with an eagle on top and a dragon below in the background, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Little Hnossa, the child of Freya, was the youngest of all the Dwellers in Asgard. Of all the places she loved best, the Rainbow Bridge came first. There she would sit for hours beside Heimdall, the Watcher of the Gods, and listen to his stories. Heimdall had a horn called the Gialarhorn, and its sound could be heard through all the worlds. He had taught his ears to hear the grasses grow. His eyes could see a hundred miles around, by night as well as by day. He never slept. He told Hnossa that nine wave sisters of the sea were his nine mothers.
New word: Heimdall — the Watcher of the Gods at the Rainbow Bridge. He needs no sleep, he hears the grass grow, and his eyes see a hundred miles. When his great horn sounds, every world can hear it.

Heimdall had lived since the beginning of things, and he knew how all things came to be. "Before Asgard was built," he said, "earth and sea and sky were mixed together in a great empty chasm. In the north lay a land of deadly cold, and in the south a land of fire. Rivers of ice poured into the chasm, and the fire made mist and drops of dew. From those drops was formed Ymir, the Ancient Giant. A Giant Cow fed him with her milk. From drops of dew too came the first Giants, and Ymir married one of the Frost Daughters."

Then the Cow licked a cliff of salt ice, and a man's head appeared in the cliff with golden hair. Bur was formed there, the first of the heroes, and Ymir hated him for his beauty. Long after, Odin, the grandson of Bur, and his brothers fought the Ancient Giant and slew him. So much blood poured out that it drowned all his Giant brood. Only one Giant escaped, floating away in a boat with his wife. Then Odin and his brothers made the world from Ymir's vast body. His bones became the mountains, his teeth the rocks, his hair the forests, and his great hollow skull the sky.
Heimdall sits by the Rainbow Bridge with little Hnossa and tells her of the World Tree Ygdrassil.

They took the sparks of the fire land and made the sun, the moon, and the stars. Night and Day were given horses to drive across the sky, one dark and one shining. Then Odin made men and women and gave them Midgard to live in. High above it all grows Ygdrassil, the World Tree, with three great roots. An eagle who knows all things sits on its topmost bough. A dragon gnaws forever at its root below, and a squirrel runs between them carrying naughty messages. Beside one root is Mimir's Well of Wisdom. Beside another is Urda's Well, guarded by three holy sisters, where two white swans make sweet music.

Ygdrassil is the World Tree, the greatest of all trees. Its branches hold up the sky, and its three roots reach down to three worlds. Gods and Men are afraid to speak of the day when it might be destroyed.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · Odin's Sacrifice
chapters.artPrompt: a hooded wanderer with a staff bowing beside a deep well under a giant tree root, a single eye shining far below in the dark water, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Odin longed for wisdom more than for anything in the world. He laid aside his golden armor, his eagle helmet, and his spear. In a cloak of dark blue, with a staff in his hand, he traveled as Vegtam the Wanderer. On the way to Mimir's Well he met a Giant riding on a great stag. It was Vafthrudner, the wisest of the Giants, who loved a game of riddles. The stakes were high: a head for a head. "I am ready," said Odin.

New word: Vegtam the Wanderer — a secret name Odin takes when he travels among men and Giants. In a dark blue cloak and with a staff, he looks like any traveler on the road. Only his wisdom gives him away.

The Giant asked the name of the river that divides Asgard from Joetunheim, and Odin answered rightly. He asked next the names of the horses of Day and Night, and again the Wanderer knew. Then it was Odin's turn. "What will be the last words that Odin will whisper into the ear of Baldur, his dear son?" he asked. The Giant sprang from his stag, for only Odin could ask that question. "You are Odin, and your question I cannot answer," he said. So Odin let him keep his head, and asked one thing more. What price would Mimir ask for a draught from the Well of Wisdom? "Your right eye," said Vafthrudner, "and no less."

A terrible price it seemed, and Odin almost turned back to Asgard. But he looked south and saw the fire land, where Surtur waits with a flaming sword. He looked north and heard the roaring of the dark land of cold. "The world must not be left between fire and darkness," he thought. "I must win the wisdom that will help to save it." So he came at last to Mimir's Well, deep under the great root of the World Tree. Old Mimir sat beside the water, with his deep eyes bent upon it, and he knew who stood before him.
Odin bows his head beside Mimir's Well while his eye shines deep in the dark water.

Many had come to the well, Mimir said, but none had ever paid the price. Odin said that he would not shrink from it. Mimir filled a great horn with water from the well and gave it to him. Odin drank and drank, and as he drank all the future became clear to him. He saw the sorrows that would fall upon Gods and men, and how they might be borne nobly. Then he put his hand to his face and plucked out his right eye. He made no sound of pain. Mimir took the eye and sank it deep in the well. And there it shines up through the water to this day. It is the sign of the price the Father of the Gods paid for wisdom.

Mimir's Well is the Well of Wisdom, deep under a root of the World Tree. Whoever drinks from it sees things that are to come. Its keeper is Mimir, the wisest being in the world, and wisdom always has a price.
